passage: "Vishal, your jaw is doing it again," Rajni said, setting down two mugs on the kitchen counter. "Doing what?" "Clenching. Look, your cheeks are hard." Vishal touched his face. "I didn't notice." "You've done it since the exam schedule came out. At first I thought you were angry with me." He gave a short laugh. "With you? No. It's the placement forms. Every time I open the file my whole face goes tight." "Want me to sit with you while you fill them?" "Yes, please." Rajni pulled up a chair. "Try dropping your shoulders." Vishal breathed out and his jaw loosened. "That is much better. Thanks for asking instead of just being annoyed."

qa.q: What has Vishal been doing since the exam schedule came out?
qa.a: He has been clenching his jaw.

qa.q: What did Rajni first think about Vishal's clenched jaw, and what was Vishal really feeling?
qa.a: Rajni first thought he might be angry with her, but Vishal was actually worried about the placement forms. He had not even noticed his jaw.

qa.q: What could Rajni and Vishal do to ease the tension while filling forms?
qa.a: Sit together, drop the shoulders, breathe out slowly, and take breaks as needed.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt when she thought Vishal was angry with her?
qa.a: She probably felt uneasy or hurt, which is why asking him was a relief.

grounding: A young adult clenches the jaw under stress, others may read anger, but it is worry, and a check-in helps.

passage: When I was preparing for my final viva, my roommate Anjali said gently, "Elizabeth, your jaw is like stone." I hadn't realised I was grinding my teeth in my sleep and clenching all day. My dentist confirmed the wear. I had thought people avoided me because I looked angry, and in a way they did; my supervisor asked once, "Are you displeased with me?" I wasn't. I was afraid I'd fail. I laughed in surprise and said, "It's just fear in my face." After that, Anjali would tap her own jaw when she saw mine tighten, and I'd unclench and breathe. It didn't remove the worry, but it stopped me looking like a storm.

qa.q: What did the supervisor ask Elizabeth?
qa.a: "Are you displeased with me?"

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when her jaw was clenched during viva preparation?
qa.a: She was afraid she would fail, which showed up as clenching. Others read it as anger, which it was not.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do to manage the clenching?
qa.a: Use the tap signal from Anjali to remind her to unclench and breathe, and see a dentist or doctor if it continues to bother her.

qa.q: How might the supervisor have seen Elizabeth's tight face?
qa.a: They may have read it as anger or displeasure, since they asked if she was upset, not knowing it was worry.

grounding: A young adult clenches the jaw when stressed, others read anger, but it reflects worry, and a kind check-in helps.

passage: Dear Urmila, thank you for meeting me before the negotiation yesterday. I did what you said and kept my face still, even when the seller named a price that made my heart jump. I wanted the flat so much, and I knew showing it would raise the price. It worked; I got it lower. But I noticed something in the corridor after. The seller seemed cold to me, and I wondered whether my blank face had made her think I didn't care. So I thanked her warmly and said I looked forward to being her neighbour. She smiled properly at last. So I'll keep the neutral face for numbers and let my words be warm. Sumit

qa.q: What did Sumit do with his face during the negotiation?
qa.a: He kept it still, even when the seller named a price that made his heart jump.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling behind his neutral face?
qa.a: He was very eager to get the flat and excited, but wanted to avoid showing it. He also worried that a blank face might seem cold.

qa.q: What did Sumit do after the negotiation to protect trust?
qa.a: He thanked the seller warmly and said he looked forward to being her neighbour.

qa.q: How might the seller have seen Sumit's blank face?
qa.a: She may have thought he did not care or was cold, until his warm words made her smile.

grounding: A young adult keeps the face neutral in a negotiation to avoid revealing eagerness, and warmth in words protects trust.

passage: "In my first deal, my face gave everything away," Uday said, leaning back in his chair while the podcast recorder ran. "The supplier saw my eyes light up at the offer, and the price went up. So the next time I practised a neutral face in front of the mirror. Harsha, my business partner, told me it made me look like a statue. In the next negotiation I kept my face calm but I added, 'I really appreciate your time and I like your work.' The supplier relaxed. Afterwards Harsha said, 'You looked cool and sounded warm.' I said, 'That's the trick.' It's a legitimate tactic as long as the warmth is real.'"

qa.q: What did the supplier see in Uday's first deal?
qa.a: The supplier saw Uday's eyes light up at the offer.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he kept his face neutral in the second negotiation?
qa.a: He was probably still eager and excited, but hid it to avoid raising the price, while he chose warm words so the supplier would not feel he was cold.

qa.q: What is a wise balance for a negotiator?
qa.a: Keep the face calm, but let warm and honest words show respect so trust is not damaged.

qa.q: How might the supplier have felt about a statue-like face?
qa.a: They may have felt uneasy, not knowing what he thought, which is why the warm words mattered.

grounding: A young adult keeps the face neutral in negotiation, a legitimate tactic, and warmth in words helps trust.

passage: Keerthana told me that Sahil, her flatmate, barely changes his expression. In the kitchen he stirs his dal with a still face, and when the group gasped at the surprise cake, he only tilted his head slightly. New friends sometimes think he is bored or cold. But I have seen how he talks: "This is the best day I've had in months," he said quietly, and put a hand on her shoulder. Keerthana said he is autistic and that his face is not a reliable clue to what he feels. She learned to listen to his words and to ask, "How was that for you?" Sahil answers plainly, and she trusts what he says more than his face.

qa.q: What did Sahil stir in the kitchen?
qa.a: Dal.

qa.q: What might new friends wrongly think about Sahil's still face?
qa.a: They may think he is bored or cold, but Sahil actually feels strongly, as his words about the best day show. His face is not a reliable guide to what he feels.

qa.q: What can friends do to understand someone with a flat facial expression?
qa.a: Listen to their words, ask plainly how something was for them and trust the answer.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel about people judging his feelings by his face?
qa.a: He may find it frustrating or lonely when people misread him, which is why his friend's plain questions help.

grounding: A young adult with a limited facial expression may feel strongly, and friends listen to words instead of judging by face.

passage: Day one. Pankaj started his new job at the library, and his colleague Hrithik noticed that his face showed almost nothing. Hrithik wondered if Pankaj disliked the team. Day four. Pankaj said in the tea break, "I want you to know I have a flat face because of how I am, and I am autistic. I feel a lot, I just don't show it in my face." Hrithik said, "Thanks for telling me. Should I ask how you are?" Pankaj said, "Yes, please." Day ten. At the team lunch, Hrithik asked, "How was that meeting for you?" Pankaj said, "It was very good; I was excited." Hrithik smiled. He trusted the words.

qa.q: What did Pankaj tell Hrithik about himself on day four?
qa.a: He said he has a flat face because of how he is, that he is autistic, and that he feels a lot but does not show it in his face.

qa.q: What did Hrithik feel and think about Pankaj's flat face at first?
qa.a: He wondered whether Pankaj disliked the team, but Pankaj actually felt a lot. His face just did not show it.

qa.q: What could Hrithik and Pankaj do to keep understanding each other?
qa.a: Hrithik can keep asking directly how things were, and Pankaj can answer in words, as they agreed.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt telling Hrithik about being autistic?
qa.a: He may have felt nervous but also relieved, especially when Hrithik thanked him.

grounding: A young adult with a flat facial expression, including autistic people, may still feel strongly, and colleagues ask and listen to words.

subtype: Lifting the chin and lowering the head [Interpreting]
passage: On the ferry crossing from Tel Aviv, Noa noticed Hiroshi, a fellow exchange student, standing at the railing with his chin lifted high as he talked to the captain. She thought, Proud, maybe even challenging. But then later, in the ship's cafe, Hiroshi sat with his head lowered while a group joked in a language he was still learning. Noa wondered whether this was deference or sadness. She had read that lifted chins and lowered heads are clues, not conclusions. So she brought him a cup of tea and said, "That was a lot of new words. How are you doing?" He looked up and gave a small smile. "Tired, but happy. Thank you."

qa.q: Where did Noa see Hiroshi with his chin lifted?
qa.a: At the railing on the ferry.

qa.q: What did Noa think Hiroshi's lifted chin and lowered head might mean?
qa.a: She thought the lifted chin might mean pride or challenge and the lowered head could be deference or sadness, but she treated them as clues only. Hiroshi later said he was tired but happy.

qa.q: What worked in the way Noa checked on Hiroshi?
qa.a: She brought tea and asked a simple question about how he was doing, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi have felt among the group speaking a language he was learning?
qa.a: He was probably tired from keeping up with new words, and lowering his head may have been a way to rest and concentrate.

grounding: A young adult reads a lifted chin as pride and a lowered head as deference or sadness but treats them as clues among many.

subtype: Lifting the chin and lowering the head [Interpreting]
passage: In the hostel common room the quarterly meeting had begun. Swati saw Yogesh lift his chin when he disagreed with the warden about the curfew. She thought, He is challenging. He lifted his chin again when he said, "May I suggest an alternative?" Her friend leaned over: "He always holds his head like that." Later, when the warden explained the security reasons, Yogesh lowered his head, and Swati wondered if he was sad or respectful. She turned to him afterwards and asked, "What did you think of her answer?" He said, "Fair enough. I was thinking about my sister who travels at night." Swati nodded. One cue was never the whole story.

qa.q: What did Yogesh ask the warden?
qa.a: He asked, "May I suggest an alternative?"

qa.q: What did Swati first think Yogesh's lifted chin meant?
qa.a: She thought he was challenging the warden, but her friend said he always holds his head that way. Later she was unsure whether his lowered head meant sadness or respect.

qa.q: What could Swati do rather than decide from his chin?
qa.a: She can ask him what he thought, as she did, and consider his words and the context.

qa.q: How might the warden have seen Yogesh's lifted chin?
qa.a: She may have taken it as a challenge, though it could just be his usual posture.

grounding: A young adult reads a lifted chin as pride or challenge and a lowered head as deference or sadness, as one clue among many.

passage: Sunday night, my diary. Today Lakshmi's Bulgarian flatmate Petya asked whether I wanted to join her for dinner, and I nodded and said "mm." She asked again and then looked confused. I realised my head wobble means yes, and in Bulgaria her nod and her head-shake mean the opposite of what I expect. So when she nodded, I thought she was refusing! I laughed and said, "Sorry, let me use words." She said, "Yes, words!" We had soup at nine. My sister Sangeeta will love this story. I'm writing it down so I don't forget: where a nod may mean I am listening, not I agree, ask.

qa.q: What time did they have soup?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi think when Petya nodded, and why?
qa.a: She thought Petya was refusing, because in Bulgaria the meanings of nod and shake are reversed compared to what she expected. She realised it once they talked.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi do in cross-cultural talks with nodding?
qa.a: Use words to clarify, like saying yes or no aloud.

qa.q: How might Petya have felt when Lakshmi wobbled her head and then looked confused?
qa.a: Petya probably felt puzzled at first, then amused once they sorted out the confusion.

grounding: A young adult learns that a nod can mean different things across cultures, such as in Bulgaria, and clarifies with words.

subtype: Raised shoulders as fear or cold [Interpreting]
passage: "Ira, I saw someone once with their shoulders up by their ears," said Pema, who was seventy, as they waited for the bus in Darjeeling's cold. "I thought, that girl is frightened. I nearly went to her and asked what was wrong. But I looked at the way she held her arms and the breath making clouds, and I thought, Is she just cold?" Ira, her granddaughter, was zipping up her jacket. "Which was it?" "Cold. She said, 'Thanks, I'm freezing.' I gave her my shawl. If I had guessed fear I would have made her feel silly." Ira smiled. "So you ask?" "First look at the weather. Then ask."

qa.q: Where were Pema and Ira waiting for the bus?
qa.a: In Darjeeling in the cold.

qa.q: What did Pema first think when she saw the girl with raised shoulders?
qa.a: She thought the girl was frightened, but then considered she might just be cold. The girl said she was freezing.

qa.q: What is a good approach when someone's shoulders are raised?
qa.a: Look at the context, like the weather, and ask before assuming fear or worry.

qa.q: How might the girl have felt if Pema had assumed she was frightened?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed or silly, since she was only cold.

grounding: A young adult sees raised shoulders and might guess fear, but it may be cold, so context and asking come first, told as an elder's memory.

subtype: Raised shoulders as fear or cold [Interpreting]
passage: The wind on the ferry platform was fierce and the ticket queue crept forward. Chaitanya, twenty, noticed a woman in front of him hunched with her shoulders lifted and her hands in her sleeves. Was she scared of the crossing? Or of something else? His friend Lalit whispered, "Maybe she's just cold. It's freezing." Chaitanya took a breath and said, "Excuse me, the wind is strong. Are you okay?" She turned and smiled. "Just cold, thank you. I forgot my scarf." He pulled off his own and offered it; she hesitated, then accepted. "Thank you. You are kind." Lalit grinned. "See? Ask first." The ferry horn sounded, and they shuffled aboard.

qa.q: What did the woman say she had forgotten?
qa.a: Her scarf.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya worried about when he saw the woman with raised shoulders?
qa.a: He wondered whether she was scared of the crossing or something else, but Lalit suggested she might just be cold. She confirmed she was cold.

qa.q: What worked in how Chaitanya approached the woman?
qa.a: He asked politely if she was okay, and then offered his scarf, without assuming why she was hunched.

qa.q: How might the woman have felt when a stranger asked about her?
qa.a: She probably felt a little surprised and then grateful for the kindness.

grounding: A young adult sees a person with raised shoulders and may guess fear, but it may be cold, so context and asking come first.

passage: At the village panchayat hall near Nashik, the exchange student Nikita was presenting a water-saving plan. When she asked the older men whether they liked it, one of them shrugged slowly, shoulders up, and looked away. Nikita's heart sank. Tanuja, the sarpanch's daughter, saw her face and whispered, "That is Bapu's way of saying he has to think." Nikita, who came from a place where a shrug could mean not caring at all, asked aloud, "Bapu, shall I explain again?" He smiled, "Please. Slower." She did, and this time he nodded and asked about the costs. After the meeting Tanuja said, "In your country a shrug is rude, isn't it?" "Sometimes," said Nikita. "I should have asked."

qa.q: Where was Nikita presenting the plan?
qa.a: At the village panchayat hall near Nashik.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel when the older man shrugged?
qa.a: She felt discouraged, because in her country a shrug can mean not caring. Tanuja explained it meant he was thinking.

qa.q: What worked in how Nikita responded to the shrug?
qa.a: She asked out loud if she should explain again, and that opened a real conversation.

qa.q: How might Bapu have seen his own shrug?
qa.a: He probably meant it as a sign he was thinking, and was pleased Nikita took time to explain slowly.

grounding: A young adult finds that a shrug carries different weight across cultures, and words prevent misunderstanding.

passage: In the seminar room at the management institute in Delhi, Maria adjusted her slides and took a breath. In the practice sessions, her coach had said: keep your arms open and relaxed, and avoid crossing them tightly; it makes people feel welcome. Maria let her arms hang loose and gestured gently towards the chart. Simran, sitting in the second row, uncrossed her own arms without noticing. But after the talk Maria went to the corridor and let out a big breath, hands trembling. Simran followed. "You looked so calm." Maria laughed. "I felt like a rabbit. I just practised the arms." Simran said, "Skill, not magic." Maria grinned. "Exactly."

qa.q: In which row did Simran sit?
qa.a: In the second row.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling while she kept her arms open and relaxed?
qa.a: She was nervous, like a rabbit, but used the arm position as a practised skill. Her trembling hands afterwards show the calm was partly performance.

qa.q: What could Maria do to keep improving her presentations?
qa.a: Keep practising the open posture and also work on calming her nerves with breathing and preparation.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt watching Maria's open arms?
qa.a: She probably felt welcome and relaxed, and even uncrossed her own arms.

grounding: A young adult presenting keeps open, relaxed arms and avoids stiff crossing, and it is a skill, not a guarantee of confidence.

passage: "You did the arms thing," Vasudha said, walking out of the auditorium with Parul. "What arms thing?" "Open, relaxed. Not crossed. It made me feel welcome. I stopped hiding behind my notes because you didn't hide either." Parul laughed. "My hands were shaking, you know. I told myself: arms open, it's a habit." "You looked calm." "Looks can lie, or at least half-lie." Vasudha said, "Is it a trick then?" "A skill," said Parul. "Like handwriting. It doesn't make you confident, but it lets people in." She flexed her fingers. "Now I need tea." Vasudha said, "Good tip: open arms at the audience, closed fists at the kettle." They laughed together.

qa.q: What did Parul say she needed after the talk?
qa.a: She said she needed tea.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling while she kept her arms open?
qa.a: She was nervous, with shaking hands, but used open arms as a habit to welcome the audience. The look of calm did not match how she felt inside.

qa.q: What could Vasudha take from Parul's example?
qa.a: Practise open, relaxed arms as a skill for welcoming an audience, while understanding it does not guarantee confidence.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel as an audience member?
qa.a: She felt welcome and less inclined to hide behind her notes.

grounding: A young adult presenting keeps open, relaxed arms and avoids stiff crossing, which is a skill and not a guarantee of confidence.

subtype: Raised arms in celebration or surrender [Mismatch]
passage: Day one. In Imphal, Damini and Lalremsiami went to the hockey final. Lalremsiami watched the last goal go in and Damini threw both arms high, screaming. Day three. At the clinic, Damini was asked to raise her arms for a check, and she lifted them slowly, saying, "Surrender," and laughing. Lalremsiami said, "You do that when we win too." Day five. In the office, Damini stretched, arms overhead, with a groan. A colleague across the room raised his own arms in mock triumph and grinned. Damini told Lalremsiami, "Same arms, three meanings." Lalremsiami nodded. "The noise and the place tell you which."

qa.q: Where did Damini and Lalremsiami go to watch hockey?
qa.a: To the hockey final in Imphal.

qa.q: What did Damini's raised arms mean in the different places?
qa.a: At the final they meant triumph and pride, at the clinic they were a check and a joking surrender, and at the office they were a stretch. The setting and noise showed which.

qa.q: What could someone do to read raised arms correctly?
qa.a: Look at the context, such as noise, setting and expression, and ask if unsure.

qa.q: How might the colleague who copied Damini's stretch have seen it?
qa.a: He took it lightly and made a joke, treating the raised arms as playful triumph.

grounding: A young adult raises the arms in triumph at a goal, in surrender or in stretching, and context shows which.

subtype: Raised arms in celebration or surrender [Mismatch]
passage: "When I was young, Jasleen, arms in the air meant many things," said Rajni, who coached the college team, tapping her whistle. "At our final I raised my arms when the winning goal went in, and the crowd roared. Two days later I raised them in the doctor's room and he said, 'Good, hold still.' A week after that I raised them at the bus stop, stretching, and a stranger thought I was celebrating and clapped. I was mortified and pleased." Jasleen laughed. "So how do you tell?" "The noise, the setting, the face. When in doubt, ask. But at a goal, I don't need to. The whole stadium tells you." She smiled.

qa.q: What did the doctor say when Rajni raised her arms?
qa.a: He said, "Good, hold still."

qa.q: What might the stranger at the bus stop have thought when Rajni stretched, and how did Rajni feel?
qa.a: The stranger thought she was celebrating and clapped, and Rajni felt mortified and a little pleased. The same movement can mean triumph, a medical check or a stretch.

qa.q: What can a young person learn from this story about reading raised arms?
qa.a: To look at context like noise and setting, and to ask when unsure.

qa.q: How might the stranger have felt after clapping?
qa.a: They may have felt amused or embarrassed at misreading the stretch.

grounding: A young adult raises the arms in triumph at a goal, in medical settings and in stretching, and context shows which, told as an elder's story.

subtype: Clenched fists and tense hands in conflict [Interpreting]
passage: Day one. Manoj saw Siddharth's clenched fists as they argued about the shared kitchen rota. He felt his own chest tighten. Instead of raising his voice, he said, "Let's stop for a moment. I can see you are upset." Siddharth's shoulders eased slightly, but the fists stayed. Day two. The flatmates spoke again with a third friend present, who kept the tone calm; Siddharth's hands were open on the table. Day four. Manoj noticed Siddharth's fists tighten while carrying two heavy bags in the cold. He asked, "Shall I take one?" Siddharth said, "Thanks. It's freezing." Manoj realised a tight fist may also come from effort or the weather, but he was glad he had kept his distance and used calm words during the argument.

qa.q: What did Manoj say when he saw Siddharth's clenched fists?
qa.a: He said, "Let's stop for a moment. I can see you are upset."

qa.q: What did Manoj think Siddharth's clenched fists showed during the argument?
qa.a: He took them as a possible warning of anger, so he calmed his own voice and kept his distance. Later he saw clenched hands can also mean effort or cold.

qa.q: What could Manoj do if a heated argument gets worse?
qa.a: Keep his distance, use calm words and involve a third person or another helper.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt when Manoj named that he was upset?
qa.a: He probably felt heard, since his shoulders eased a little, though his fists stayed for a while.

grounding: A young adult sees clenched fists in a heated exchange as a possible warning and chooses distance, calm words and help, while noting fists can also mean effort or cold.

subtype: Clenched fists and tense hands in conflict [Interpreting]
passage: "I once saw a man clench his fists in the middle of a heated argument at the bus depot," Varun told his nephew Nitin on the railway platform. "I was twenty. My first thought was to shout back. But the fists frightened me, and I remembered my mother telling me to take one step back and speak calmly. So I stepped back, lowered my voice, and asked a bystander to stay close. The man's fists loosened. Later I saw the same fists gripping a heavy sack; he was tired. I still don't know if he wanted to hurt anyone. But I learned that distance and calm words are never wasted." Nitin nodded. "And getting help." "Yes. That first."

qa.q: Where did Varun see the man clench his fists?
qa.a: At the bus depot.

qa.q: What did Varun feel when he saw the clenched fists, and what did he do?
qa.a: He felt frightened and thought of shouting back, but he remembered his mother's advice, stepped back and spoke calmly. He treated the fists as a possible warning.

qa.q: What can a person do when they see clenched fists in an argument?
qa.a: Step back, speak calmly and ask others nearby for help.

qa.q: How might the man have felt while arguing at the depot?
qa.a: He was probably angry or tired, and the same fists later gripping a sack shows they could also mean effort.

grounding: A young adult sees clenched fists in a heated exchange as a possible warning and chooses distance, calm words and help, told by an elder.
